prize_parts.citation: for building modern political economics by analysing how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic development

statement.case_for: B016 is a field-creating contribution. It joins formal theory on how political incentives, electoral rules and constitutions determine fiscal policy and public-goods provision with empirical work on those outcomes. It also covers state capacity, accountability and taxation. Its reach into public finance, macro and development is broad, and the framework has been confirmed, extended and taught for about three decades. In my opening I proposed only Persson and Tabellini. Colleagues' arguments, in particular Friberg's, have led me to add Besley. The state-capacity strand is part of the discovery as listed, and the Besley-Persson and Persson-Tabellini programmes are tightly interlinked. Omitting Besley would make the citation narrower than the contribution. A three-person set therefore gives the cleanest attribution available within the limit, while Acemoglu and Robinson, who are outside this ballot, are already laureates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical credibility. Part of the evidence on constitutional and electoral-rule effects rests on observational cross-country variation, so it is less secure than the theory. A second reservation is thematic proximity to the 2024 institutions prize, which could make this seem less urgent. Third, B016 has fewer ranked supporters than B014 or B032, so it may not command broad agreement once the discussion turns to the full ballot.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B016 first as the creation of modern political economics. He credits Persson and Tabellini with theory and comparative constitutions and Besley with state capacity, and he notes the three-person cap is a clean but imperfect cut because Acemoglu, Robinson and Alesina sit outside it.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and have revised my opening in light of it. I had left Besley out to keep the award to two. Friberg is right that state capacity is a distinct and independently strong strand, and the citation should cover it. I would still qualify one point: omitted contributors such as Alesina are a reason to write the citation around the specific programmes of electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity, rather than around the whole field.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B016 third. He warns that proximity to the 2024 institutions prize may lower its priority and that causal identification in the cross-country constitutional evidence is contested.
responses.response: I take the identification point seriously and think it limits how strongly the empirical claims can be stated. The 2024 prize concerned colonial-origin institutions and long-run prosperity. B016 concerns how political rules and capacity shape fiscal and policy choices within existing states, so I read the overlap as partial rather than duplicative. I accept that this judgement is contestable. It is the main reason B016 is not clearly dominant over the macro alternatives.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B042 first. He sees Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) as the clearly attributable origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism, with a tight two-person credit. He flags the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as a possible overlap and notes that direct empirical validation is weaker than the theoretical influence.
responses.response: I rank B042 second and agree that attribution is its main strength. It is cleaner than B016's attribution. I also agree that the 2022 prize covered neighbouring but different ground, so I do not see the overlap as disqualifying. I keep B042 as an alternative because the mechanism rests mostly on theory and calibration, with mixed identification of the collateral channel. B016 offers a wider body of confirmed theory and evidence, even though its attribution is less tidy. If the Committee weights attribution cleanliness above breadth, B042 is the natural second path.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first. He argues that the New Keynesian framework is the standard basis for monetary policy analysis, that the contribution is conceptual and practical, and that the 2022 inflation episode has not undermined the core. He regards the timing as arguably overdue, with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as the core trio.
responses.response: I agree that B014's impact on policy practice is very large, and I ranked it third with the same trio. My reservation is attribution. With eight credited names, a three-person cut necessarily excludes Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, whose empirical and medium-scale DSGE contributions are substantial. 'Overdue' is also a statement about timing, not about how credit should be divided. I would want the Committee to settle whether the prize honours the theoretical core or the estimated-model strand before treating B014 as ready. That is why I list it as an alternative rather than as my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: How much weight the Committee should give to the partly observational cross-country identification behind the constitutional and electoral-rule findings.
Whether the 2024 institutions prize makes B016 less pressing, or whether its focus on fiscal and policy outcomes within states is distinct enough.

Whether Besley's addition is better supported than the two-person Persson-Tabellini configuration I proposed in my opening, and whether other political-economy contributors outside the ballot affect the attribution.
Whether B042's cleaner attribution should outweigh B016's breadth, and how the Committee would treat the 2022 prize in that comparison.
The scientific and attribution case for B014 depends on a three-person cut among eight credited names, which I cannot resolve with the evidence supplied.
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile documents no co-authorship, institutional tie or other connection to the credited names on B016, B042 or B014. My opening noted a possible IIES connection with Persson, but that affiliation is not in the supplied profile, so I disclose it as possible and unverified, not as established. The profile does document my dynamic political-economy work with Storesletten, Zilibotti, Rodríguez Mora and Krusell. That work is adjacent to B016's field, and none of those coauthors is credited on any shortlisted ballot. My ties to committee members Boppart, Friberg and Krusell are coauthorship and IIES colleagueship, and none of them is a credited name. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
